## Evidence: the crash is intermittent, not a deterministic regression

`build-and-test / pytest (ubuntu-latest, py3.11)` **passed** on `main` at the same
commit the crash was observed against.

- Crashing run: 35510440501 (change 3008 patch set 1, rev `f2200580a17e`), py3.11 leg
  crashed `gw3` on `test_worker_cancellation_survives_job_completion_race`.
- Passing run: 35511654149 `Test Suite (mirror)`, head `e84e4c5e943`, job
  106080485643 `build-and-test / pytest (ubuntu-latest, py3.11)` -> **success**.

`f2200580a17e` is change 3008 applied on top of `e84e4c5e943`, and change 3008 touches
only `.github/workflows/external-integration.yml`. So the two runs exercise effectively
identical Python code on the same interpreter leg, and one crashed while the other did
not.

This rules out a deterministic regression of `8c9bf5d78d` and confirms the failure is a
low-rate race. It also means a reproduction attempt must be a LOOP, not a single run --
one green run is not evidence of absence. The prior RCA's own oracle needed 3 runs to
show 2 hangs, so the historical rate is high enough to catch in tens of runs but not in
one.

## Sweep context

`main` currently carries no other unexplained CI failure. Non-green runs as of
2026-09-20T13:15Z:

| Run | Workflow | State | Attribution |
|---|---|---|---|
| 35510440501 | change 3008 Verified gate | failure | THIS ticket |
| 35507409132 | Terraform Drift | failure | known, awaiting user decision (`[rebar:3d85-eaad-b5e0-4f84]`) |
| 35508005436 | Live External Integration | in progress | healthy; DC harness at 1h43m vs a 6252s green baseline |
| 35511654149 | Test Suite (mirror) | in progress | py3.11 leg already green |
| 35512947017 | Mirror Guard | in progress | - |

A differential reproduction on a dedicated Python 3.11.16 environment is now running
(the repo `.venv` is 3.12.14 and cannot discriminate a 3.11-only defect).

comments.author: Rebar Bot
comments.body:
## Implementation finding: `asyncio.timeout` cannot bound this join

My first cut of the bounded teardown helper used `asyncio.timeout(bound)` around
`await worker`. **It does not bound anything**, and the new regression test proved it by
hanging for the full 30s suite budget.

`asyncio.timeout` and `asyncio.wait_for` both work by *cancelling the inner await and then
waiting for that cancellation to be honoured*. A worker that swallows cancellation — the
exact failure this guard exists to catch — never honours it, so the timeout never fires.
The guard was therefore vacuous against its own target case.

`asyncio.wait({worker}, timeout=bound)` is the only correct primitive here: it does NOT
cancel what it waits on, and it returns once the bound expires regardless of the task's
state. The helper now uses it, with that reasoning recorded at the definition site.

A second consequence, found the same way: `await task` propagates cancellation *into* the
task, so an `asyncio.timeout` join also silently consumed the test fixture's swallow budget.
The first version of the regression test asserted on final task state and failed for this
reason — the assertion was over-specified.

## Regression test is structural, not wall-clock

`scripts/check_wall_clock_asserts.py` rejects upper-bound elapsed-time asserts as a known
CI flake class, and it was right to: the test now asserts that the join **returned while
the worker is still running**, which an unbounded join could never do. No timing budget, so
nothing to flake under runner contention. A counter proves a cancellation was actually
swallowed, so the scenario cannot silently stop being exercised.

## Status

- 10/10 tests pass in `tests/unit/test_opcert_service_app.py` (1.15s; the regression test
  hits its 0.2s bound exactly).
- Verified the test FAILS (hangs) against the incorrect `asyncio.timeout` implementation —
  so it genuinely guards the property.
- `make check` green: ruff, ruff-format, mypy (771 files), zizmor, actionlint,
  MCP/library parity, comment hygiene, raw-git-writes, wall-clock-asserts, import-convention.
- `make verify` running now.

Note: these tests need the `reviewbot` extra (`fastapi` + `httpx`) or the whole module is
skipped by `importorskip`. `make install` does not pull it, so a bare worktree silently
skips all 10 tests — worth knowing before trusting a local green run on this file.

comments.body:
## Pushed — Gerrit change 3009

Commit `2da950d6b99`, Change-Id `Ib9420b6a9ba6cb62d29ac6911e5ed189ad2ba981`.
https://rebar.solutions.navateam.com/c/rebar/+/3009

## `make verify`: clean

`34 failed, 20335 passed, 80 skipped in 1811.15s`. **Zero failures attributable to this
change.** The 34 break down as 17 known-environmental pandoc failures plus 17 that were an
artifact of my own venv, described below.

Worth noting for the baseline: the expected 18th failure,
`test_completion_gate.py::test_file_impact_close_fetches_before_rejecting_stale_clone`
(bug 9753-647b), **no longer fails** — change 2989 has merged.

## The 17 extra failures were mine, not the tree's

Every test in `tests/unit/test_audit_ticket_page.py` and
`tests/unit/test_audit_ticket_page_heldout.py` failed with:

    src/rebar/audit/server.py:47: ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'jinja2'

Cause: to exercise these opcert tests at all I had to install the `reviewbot` extra
(`fastapi` + `httpx`), because `tests/unit/test_opcert_service_app.py` opens with
`pytest.importorskip("fastapi")` and `make install` does not pull that extra — so on a bare
worktree **all 10 of these tests silently skip**, and a local green run on this file means
nothing.

The audit-page tests guard on `fastapi` and `httpx` but their render path also needs
`jinja2`, which ships in the `[ui]` extra rather than `[reviewbot]`. Installing one extra
therefore un-skipped tests whose remaining dependency was still missing.

Confirmed by installing `jinja2` and re-running exactly those two files: **17 passed**. So
this is an artifact of a partial-extra install I created, not a defect in the tree and not a
regression from this change — under any sanctioned install matrix (`[ui]`, or CI's full
install) the dependency is present. Not filing a ticket for it; the guard is correct for the
install combinations the project actually supports.

## Verification summary

- 10/10 in `tests/unit/test_opcert_service_app.py`; the regression test hits its 0.2s bound.
- Regression test confirmed to FAIL (hang to the suite budget) against the incorrect
  `asyncio.timeout` implementation, so it genuinely guards the property.
- `make check` green; `make verify` clean of real failures.

Unverified: that the py3.11 `node down` crash itself stops recurring. It never reproduced
locally across 100 runs on 3.11.16/3.11.15/3.12.14, so this change is justified as a fix for
a separate and provable defect — an unbounded teardown join plus a budget that violated
pyproject's documented requirement — whose effect is to make the underlying race **legible**
rather than to mask it. If the race recurs, it will now surface as a named assertion instead
of a dead xdist worker.

comments.body:
## Bounded-loop reproduction evidence on a real 3.11 venv

The completion verifier returned FAIL with 5 of 8 criteria unmet, all of them about
reproduction evidence that had never been captured. It is right that it was missing. Here it
is, measured rather than asserted, including the part that does not flatter the fix.

### The loop, and its exact command

Interpreter: `Python 3.11.16` (`.rebar/scratch/py311-repro-43727/venv-3.11.16`), the same
patch release the crashing CI cell runs. Both arms ran under xdist to stay faithful to CI's
execution shape — the failure signature is a *worker* crash, so a non-xdist run cannot
produce it at all.

    PYTHONPATH="$tree/src" python -m pytest \
      tests/unit/test_opcert_service_app.py -n 4 -p no:randomly -q

Each iteration was wall-clock bounded at 90s so a hang would be counted rather than waited
on; rc 124/142 was classified as a hang, and worker-crash text was matched separately.

| Arm | Tree | Iterations | pass | crash | hang | other |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| PRE-FIX | `e84e4c5e943` (parent of the fix) | 40 | **40** | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| POST-FIX | `641531e62e5` (the merged fix) | 40 | **40** | 0 | 0 | 0 |

### What this establishes, and what it does not

**Reproduction rate on this host is 0/40 pre-fix.** Combined with the earlier 0/100 across
3.11.16 / 3.11.15 / 3.12.14, that is 0 reproductions in 140 local attempts against code that
*provably crashed in CI*. So the honest conclusion is not "the fix works" — it is that **this
host cannot reproduce the defect at all**, in either arm, and therefore the local loop has no
discriminating power between them.

That matters more than a green post-fix column would. A post-fix 40/40 taken alone would
look like proof and would be worthless, because the pre-fix arm is *also* 40/40. Recording
only the post-fix number would have manufactured false confidence. The pre-fix arm is the
control that shows the local experiment is null.

### Criterion 2 — the `cancelling`-at-`queue.get()` state

It cannot be obtained, and I am stating that rather than leaving it open. The criterion asks
whether the worker task is parked at `queue.get()` in a `cancelling` state, to separate a
real cancellation-consumption defect from scheduling latency. Capturing that requires a live
reproduction to inspect. Across 140 local attempts there was none, so the discriminating
observation was never available to make. This is the second branch of the verifier's own
remediation for that criterion.

### Where the discriminating evidence actually lives: CI

The defect is CI-only, so the differential has to be run there — and it is running now, as a
natural experiment rather than a contrived one:

| Patchset | Parent | Contains the fix? | py3.11 cell |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3008 ps1 (`f2200580a17`) | `e84e4c5e943` | no | **CRASHED** — run [35510440501](https://github.com/navapbc/rebar/actions/runs/35510440501), `worker 'gw3' crashed while running tests/unit/test_opcert_service_app.py::test_worker_cancellation_survives_job_completion_race`, 1 failed / 20443 passed |
| 3008 ps2 (`db06c1257a9`) | `641531e62e5` | yes | run [35517603759](https://github.com/navapbc/rebar/actions/runs/35517603759), in progress |

Same change, same test, same matrix cell; the only difference between the two arms is
whether the fix is in the parent. That is the attribution the third criterion asks for, and
it will be conclusive in the direction CI reports — including if it reports that the crash
recurs, which would mean the teardown join was not the trigger.

### Trigger attribution, stated plainly

Not yet attributed to an interpreter patch release. The 3.11.16 / 3.11.15 / 3.12.14 sweep
was inconclusive because none of them reproduced it. The live hypothesis is **test-side
scheduling latency under CI's load** — a runner under heavier contention than this host
widens the window in which the unbounded teardown join can park forever, and an unbounded
join is the only mechanism present that converts a widened window into a dead worker rather
than a slow test. The local nulls are consistent with that (an unloaded host never widens the
window), but consistency is not proof, and I am not claiming it as one. Run 35517603759 is
the test.

Artifacts cleaned up after measurement; the pre-fix tree was a throwaway detached worktree at
`e84e4c5e943`.

compiled_state.description:
## Problem

The py3.11 xdist worker crash on `tests/unit/test_opcert_service_app.py` has
RECURRED, after the fix for it was proven to hold across 21 consecutive runs.

Change 3008 (patch set 1, `f2200580a17e`) took a `Verified -1` from run
35510440501:

    FAILED tests/unit/test_opcert_service_app.py::test_worker_cancellation_survives_job_completion_race
      - worker 'gw3' crashed while running '...'
    1 failed, 20443 passed, 80 skipped in 1076.81s

    [gw3] node down: Not properly terminated
    rebar crash guard: xdist worker=gw3 terminated abnormally: Not properly terminated
    [gw3] linux -- Python 3.11.16

This is a spurious `Verified -1`. Change 3008 edits ONLY
`.github/workflows/external-integration.yml` (one pytest verbosity flag and a
comment block); the failing job is `build-and-test / pytest`, a different
workflow, so the change cannot reach it. py3.12 and py3.13 passed on the same
tree, which is also why the code under test is not deadlocking deterministically.

## Why this is a recurrence and not a regression of the old fix

`[rebar:fade-ea90-7564-4715]` (closed `duplicate`) and its principal
`[rebar:2207-2917-e21b-42bd]` (closed `flaky`) cover the same module, the same
crash signature, and this same test by name. That RCA proved the mechanism:

> **CPython issue 86296**: on Python 3.11, `asyncio.wait_for` consumes an external
> cancellation when its child completes in the same event-loop turn. The worker then
> loops back to `queue.get()` with `cancelling()==1` while lifespan awaits it forever;
> pytest-timeout kills the worker. Python 3.12+ is unaffected.

The fix, commit `8c9bf5d78d`, replaced `asyncio.wait_for(asyncio.to_thread(...))`
with `async with asyncio.timeout(...)`.

**That fix is still present.** Verified on this tree:

- `git merge-base --is-ancestor 8c9bf5d78d origin/main` -> ancestor.
- `git merge-base --is-ancestor 8c9bf5d78d f2200580a17e` (the crashing revision) -> ancestor.
- `src/rebar/opcert_service/app.py:118` still reads
  `async with asyncio.timeout(cfg.job_timeout_seconds):`.

So the old remedy has not been reverted. Something outside it still reaches the
same end state on 3.11.

## Evidence narrowing the surviving cause

Two observations that should drive the investigation rather than be assumed:

1. **The interpreter moved.** The prior positive-control crashes ran Python
   3.11.15; this crash ran **3.11.16**. `asyncio.timeout` was introduced in 3.11
   and its cancellation handling was patched repeatedly through the 3.11.x series,
   so a 3.11.16-specific interaction is a live hypothesis and is cheap to test
   differentially.

2. **A second `wait_for` survives in the same module.** `app.py:65` still uses
   `asyncio.wait_for(asyncio.gather(*tasks, return_exceptions=True), ...)` in
   `lifespan`'s shutdown path. It is NOT on the failing test's path -- that test
   drives `_worker` directly via `asyncio.create_task` and never enters lifespan --
   so it does not explain THIS crash, but it is the same 86296-susceptible
   construct in the same file and is worth settling in the same pass.

The crash mechanism itself is already documented in `pyproject.toml`: because
`timeout_method = "thread"` expires a test with `os._exit(1)`, an over-run budget
does not report `Failed: Timeout` -- it kills the whole xdist worker with exactly
`node down: Not properly terminated`. The test carries `@pytest.mark.timeout(2)`,
and that 2s budget is what converts a stall into a process kill. Note the sibling
`test_shutdown_does_not_wait_for_an_in_flight_job` in the same file uses
`@pytest.mark.timeout(60)` for the same shutdown concern.

Do NOT simply raise the budget. A wider budget would convert the crash into a
visible failure or a pass, but if the worker is genuinely parking at `queue.get()`
with a consumed cancellation, that is a real shutdown defect in a service and the
budget is only the messenger. Establish which it is first.

## Investigation plan

The repo `.venv` is 3.12 and is non-discriminating for a 3.11-only defect; the
prior RCA built a dedicated 3.11 venv and that is the required setup here too.

1. Build a Python 3.11.16 venv and run the regression oracle
   `test_worker_cancellation_survives_job_completion_race` in a loop (the prior RCA
   used 3 runs with a 120s cap to separate `rc=124` hangs from `rc=1` failures).
2. If it reproduces, capture whether the worker task is `cancelling` and parked at
   `queue.get()` -- the prior RCA's exact discriminator.
3. Compare against 3.11.15 and 3.12 to establish whether the trigger is the patch
   release.
4. Fix the cause. Only if the cause proves to be scheduling latency with no
   cancellation consumption does the budget become the right lever, and then it
   matches the sibling's 60s and carries the one-line justification comment
   `pyproject.toml` requires.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The crash is reproduced deterministically on a 3.11 venv, or a bounded loop is recorded showing the reproduction rate.
- [ ] The evidence states whether the worker task is parked at `queue.get()` in a `cancelling` state, distinguishing a real cancellation-consumption defect from scheduling latency.
- [ ] The trigger is attributed: interpreter patch release, a code path, or test-side timing.
- [ ] The root cause is fixed at its mechanism, not by widening `@pytest.mark.timeout(2)` alone.
- [ ] `app.py:65`'s surviving `asyncio.wait_for` in `lifespan` is either converted to `asyncio.timeout` or recorded as deliberately safe with the reason.
- [ ] The regression oracle passes repeatedly on 3.11 after the fix.
- [ ] The ticket records the CI run and job ids used as evidence.
compiled_state.title: py3.11 xdist worker crash recurs on test_worker_cancellation_survives_job_completion_race despite the 86296 fix
